---
title: "23. Building a clock of your own"
---

The catalogue is other people's clocks. This is the arithmetic of fitting one,
with the numbers the published clocks actually used.

## 23.1 The objective

With $n$ samples and $p$ CpGs, $p \gg n$ always. Horvath had 8,000 samples
against 21,369 candidate probes; a modern EPIC study has 850,000 columns and a
few hundred rows. An unpenalised least-squares fit is not identifiable, because
$X^\top X$ is singular whenever $p > n$. Penalisation is what makes the problem
have an answer, not a refinement on one.

$$
\hat{\beta} = \arg\min_{\beta} \left\{ \frac{1}{2n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(y_i - \beta_0 - x_i^{\top}\beta\right)^2 + \lambda\left[\frac{1-\alpha}{2}\lVert\beta\rVert_2^2 + \alpha\lVert\beta\rVert_1\right] \right\}
$$

The two penalties do different work. The $\ell_1$ term has a corner at zero, so
its subgradient can hold a coefficient exactly at zero, which is what performs
selection. The $\ell_2$ term is smooth and shrinks correlated predictors
together rather than choosing between them, which matters because neighbouring
CpGs are strongly correlated and pure LASSO picks among them close to
arbitrarily.

| $\alpha$ | Name | Behaviour on correlated CpGs | Used by |
|---:|---|---|---|
| 1 | LASSO | Selects one per correlated group, close to arbitrarily | eFRS, the McCartney EpiScores |
| 0.5 | Elastic net | Keeps correlated groups together while still zeroing most coefficients | Horvath 2013 |
| 0 | Ridge | Shrinks everything, selects nothing | Rarely used alone |

Horvath fitted $\alpha = 0.5$ with $\lambda = 0.0226$ chosen by cross-validation,
over the 21,369 probes shared by the 27K and 450K platforms that had fewer than
ten missing values. That produced the 353 sites.

::: {.callout-important}
## The selected set is not the biology

Rerun the same fit with a slightly different $\lambda$, a different fold split,
or a different subset of samples, and a different CpG set comes out with almost
identical accuracy. The correlated groups are interchangeable to the optimiser.
This is one mechanism behind the discrepancies listed in section 15.2, and it is
why two faithful implementations of the same clock can disagree on membership.
:::

## 23.2 Choosing the penalty honestly

$\lambda$ comes from $k$-fold cross-validation: fit on $k-1$ folds, measure on
the held-out one, take the $\lambda$ minimising mean cross-validated error, or
the largest $\lambda$ within one standard error of it for a sparser model.

Any step that looked at the outcome must sit inside the loop. Selecting CpGs by
their correlation with age on the full dataset and then cross-validating the fit
on those CpGs leaks the held-out fold into the selection, and the reported error
is optimistic by an amount that cannot be recovered afterwards.

## 23.3 The age transform

Methylation changes quickly in childhood and slowly afterwards, so a model
linear in age fits adults and misses the first two decades. Horvath regresses a
transformed age and inverts afterwards, with $A = 20$. Up to $A$,

$$
F(\text{age}) = \log(\text{age} + 1) - \log(A + 1),
$$

and above it,

$$
F(\text{age}) = \frac{\text{age} - A}{A + 1}.
$$

Both branches give 0 at $\text{age} = A$ and both have derivative $1/(A+1)$
there, so $F$ is continuous and differentiable at the join. The model predicts
$F$; the reported age is $F^{-1}$ of the linear predictor. Applying the inverse
twice, or omitting it, is invisible in an adult cohort because the branches
nearly agree there, and badly wrong in a paediatric one.

## 23.4 Feature selection is not settled

Elastic net is the default rather than the optimum. Benchmarked on the Hannum
blood data (GSE40279, 656 samples, 473,035 CpGs, 10-fold cross-validation,
80/20 split):

| Method | CpGs kept | R² | Median error |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| SelectKBest (2,000) then Boruta | 35 | 0.873 | 3.08 years |
| Boruta alone, or KBest alone | varies | 0.861 to 0.862 | |
| Recursive elimination, 1% per iteration | varies | ≥ 0.81 | |
| Genetic algorithm, most threshold methods | varies | 0.77 to 0.81 | |
| Neural network on 65 features | 65 | 0.76 | found 61 CpGs no other method did |
| Elastic net, no prior selection | 276 | below five of the above | |
| The five most-selected CpGs overall | 5 | 0.83 | 3.79 years |
| cg16867657 (ELOVL2) alone | 1 | 0.73 | |

Two rows there are worth sitting with. A single CpG in ELOVL2 reaches R² = 0.73,
so most of what a 353-CpG clock knows about chronological age is available from
a handful of sites. And an unfiltered elastic net over all 473,035 probes was
beaten by five selection strategies, which is the opposite of the usual
intuition: past a point the extra probes contribute noise rather than signal.

## 23.5 Two metrics that disagree, and both are needed

$$
\text{MedAE} = \operatorname{median}_i\left|\hat{y}_i - y_i\right|, \qquad r = \operatorname{corr}(\hat{y}, y)
$$

Correlation is inflated by a wide age range and says nothing about bias. Median
absolute error is in years and says nothing about ordering. A clock at r = 0.95
on a cohort spanning 20 to 90 may have an MAE of six years; the same clock on a
cohort spanning 55 to 65 may have r near zero and the same MAE. Neither number
is wrong and neither alone is informative.

Expect the fitted slope of $\hat{y}$ on $y$ to fall below one. Penalisation
shrinks coefficients toward zero, which compresses predictions toward the
training mean, so the old read young and the young read old. That is regression
to the mean, a property of the estimator rather than a defect of the cohort, and
it leaves the residual correlated with age unless the slope is corrected. It is
why [age acceleration](../analysis/acceleration.qmd) is a residual on chronological age.

## 23.6 The step that gets skipped

A model fitted to chronological age will correlate with chronological age.
Reporting that as validation is circular. The claim worth making is about the
residual: whether age acceleration associates with disease, mortality or an
intervention, on a cohort that was not used to fit the model. Everything in
section 11 applies to a clock you fitted exactly as it applies to a published
one.

## 23.7 What to publish

Feature list, weights, intercept, the preprocessing chain and the postprocess,
together and in the order they apply. A clock published without its postprocess
is the commonest source of the disagreements in section 15, because the next
implementer has to guess whether an anti-log was already applied, and a
plausible wrong guess produces plausible wrong ages.

## 23.8 Fitting one here

`fa.fit_clock(data, target="age")` fits an elastic net to one cohort and reports only
predictions made out of fold: the cohort is split into outer folds, lambda is chosen by
cross-validation inside each training part, and each held-out fold is predicted by a model that
saw neither its samples nor their role in choosing lambda. The estimator is glmnet's for a
gaussian outcome, including its internal scaling of the outcome, its lambda grid and
`cv.glmnet`'s `lambda.1se` or `lambda.min`. It reproduces glmnet 5.1's path to within 1e-6 and
chooses exactly the lambdas that `cv.glmnet`'s rules give on glmnet's own fold fits; `cv.glmnet`'s
returned lambdas can differ slightly, because its internal fold fits differ from direct `glmnet`
calls by about 1e-4 in MSE. A missing value is filled with its feature's mean in the training part it
falls in. The model fitted on everyone is returned for new samples, and its accuracy is the
out-of-fold one, not its fit. The result is a model of this cohort and is labelled as one.
